transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Dedicated expansion check-in - commit burn-down + attribution questions
Date: 2026-02-12
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 41 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Rachel Kim, Cole Summers
Northbridge Health: Ava Thompson (Director, Data Platform), Miguel Santos (Staff ML Engineer), Priya Desai (FinOps)

---

Summary (auto-generated)
- Reviewed month-to-date commit burn and projected overage.
- Discussed how requests are attributed to commit vs overage.
- Clarified token accounting under batching and caching.
- Agreed on next steps to reconcile using request IDs.

Topics (auto-generated)
1) Commit burn-down
2) Invoice vs Console
3) Batching and caching
4) Expansion options

Action items (auto-generated)
- Rachel to send burn-down export with meter definitions.
- Customer to share request IDs for reconciliation.
- Cole to confirm cache token line item treatment under current order form.

Questions (auto-generated)
- Does batching inflate token counts?
- Are cached tokens billed the same as uncached tokens on Dedicated?
- Why does Console show a different number than the invoice preview sometimes?

---

Transcript

[00:00] Rachel Kim: Alright, I think we’re good. Thanks everyone for making time. This is our Dedicated expansion check-in. I know you all had a couple questions on the burn-down and also token accounting with caching.

[00:12] Ava Thompson: Yep. Thanks Rachel. We’re basically trying to forecast if we’re going to go over this month. And then Miguel had some questions because his numbers don’t match the console.

[00:22] Priya Desai: And I have invoice questions too. Like what actually burns down the commit versus what’s just, you know, observability.

[00:30] Rachel Kim: Great. That’s exactly the agenda. Cole is on as well—he can answer the more technical attribution questions.

[00:38] Cole Summers: Hey everyone.

[00:40] Miguel Santos: Hi.

[00:43] Rachel Kim: Cool. Let me start with where you are right now. As of yesterday end of day UTC—sorry, we can talk time zones in a sec—you’re at about 78% of the monthly commit consumed. The last three days have been a bit spiky, mostly driven by the rerank endpoint and the larger chat model you’re using in US-East.

[01:05] Priya Desai: When you say end of day UTC, that’s already one mismatch for us because our finance team is looking at Pacific.

[01:12] Rachel Kim: Yeah. Totally fair. The invoice run and the burn-down export are in UTC windows. The Console can display in local time, but the “invoice preview” mode is UTC. That’s one of the common places we see deltas.

[01:27] Ava Thompson: Ok, but the bigger concern is: we’re seeing what looks like faster burn-down after we turned on caching. That seems backwards.

[01:35] Miguel Santos: Yeah. Exactly. We enabled prefix caching for our system prompt. We expected to pay less or at least see fewer tokens. But Redwood is showing more tokens in some views.

[01:46] Cole Summers: Let’s separate two things: token counts, and compute cost. Caching reduces compute, but depending on your contract and how we meter, you might see additional token categories. It shouldn’t increase “total tokens generated,” but it can change the breakdown.

[02:02] Miguel Santos: Are you saying you’re billing cache tokens?

[02:05] Cole Summers: Not “extra” tokens. What happens is the request has input tokens and output tokens—same as usual. With caching, some portion of the input is served from cache (cache read). We record that as cache_read_tokens. The remaining prompt tokens are prompt_uncached_tokens. So you might be looking at a dashboard that sums prompt + cache read and thinks it’s “more.” But it’s really just a decomposition of the same prompt.

[02:30] Ava Thompson: Hmm. Our internal counter just counts prompt tokens. We don’t have a separate counter for cached prompt.

[02:36] Cole Summers: Right. And the other key piece: continuous batching does not inflate token counts. Batching is an execution strategy—like we’re packing multiple requests on GPU. It changes latency and throughput characteristics, not token accounting.

[02:51] Miguel Santos: Ok, but why would the commit burn faster after caching? That’s the part that makes no sense.

[02:58] Rachel Kim: I can take a first stab and Cole you can correct me. I think the burn-down report is using “billable units” per your order form. If cache read tokens are billed at the same rate in your Dedicated plan, then turning on caching won’t reduce the bill, it just reduces our GPU cost. If cache read tokens are discounted or zero-rated, then you should see burn-down slow.

[03:22] Priya Desai: Wait, so which one is it for us?

[03:25] Cole Summers: I don’t want to guess from memory. I’ll confirm against your order form and the current billing config. Some Dedicated customers have cache read tokens priced at $0 as part of the commit, others have them at a reduced rate, and some have the same rate because the commit is basically “all usage.”

[03:44] Ava Thompson: That seems… not obvious from the console.

[03:48] Rachel Kim: Agree. We’ve been improving the Console labeling so it’s clearer what maps to invoice line items. We’ll send a one-pager that explains what burns down commit.

[03:58] Miguel Santos: I’d really like to understand the exact formula. Like, what fields get multiplied by what.

[04:05] Cole Summers: Totally. High level, for Hosted it’s usually prompt tokens and completion tokens. For Dedicated, we still measure the same primitives but attribution is: (a) usage that maps to your committed pool burns down the commit, and (b) usage outside the pool, or above included amounts, becomes overage line items. Then there are request outcomes—if a request fails before any tokens are produced, it may not be billable. If tokens are produced and the client disconnects mid-stream, we bill what was actually generated up to the disconnect—no tokens after disconnect.

[04:35] Miguel Santos: On streaming—this is another mismatch. Sometimes we cancel a stream when the user navigates away. Our logs show we got, like, 200 tokens, but your console says 240.

[04:45] Cole Summers: That can happen if your client received 200 but the server generated 240 before it got the cancel signal. There’s a small race there. We bill for tokens generated and sent (or attempted to be sent) up to the disconnect detection. We don’t bill after we detect the disconnect. But your client-side count can be lower if it dropped the connection or stopped reading.

[05:10] Ava Thompson: So you bill what you generated, not what we read.

[05:14] Cole Summers: Correct. That’s standard across most providers. But again, we can reconcile it using request_id and the per-request “output_tokens” and “disconnect_reason” fields.

[05:25] Priya Desai: On retries: we do automatic retries on 429s. Are we paying twice?

[05:31] Cole Summers: If you retry a request and it produces tokens both times, then yes, that’s two billable attempts. If it fails before producing tokens, we generally don’t bill token usage, but there may still be a request count metric—depending on plan. We’re adding clearer “request_outcome” and “retry_reason” breakdowns in reporting. For now, we can isolate it by looking at request outcomes.

[05:56] Miguel Santos: We do see spikes when we hit rate limits.

[06:00] Rachel Kim: That’s consistent with what I saw too—there’s a day where your 429s jumped and then your retries jumped. It’s not huge, but it contributes.

[06:09] Ava Thompson: Ok. Back to forecasting. Are we on track to exceed the commit?

[06:15] Rachel Kim: If the last week pattern continues, yes, you’ll go over by around 12–18%. If we assume your current caching configuration and the rerank volume stays the same. There’s a big weekly batch job you run Thursdays, right?

[06:30] Miguel Santos: Yeah. We run weekly evals and then we do a re-embed for new documents.

[06:36] Priya Desai: Which is… expensive.

[06:39] Rachel Kim: Right. So two options: (1) we keep the commit as-is and you accept some overage, or (2) we increase the commit and potentially add a burst pool so you don’t pay as much overage during spikes.

[06:55] Ava Thompson: What is “burst pool” in your terms? Like extra GPUs on demand?

[07:01] Rachel Kim: Exactly. Reserved baseline capacity and then burst capacity that can come online with pre-agreed rates. It helps with end-of-quarter or batch jobs.

[07:11] Miguel Santos: If we did that, does attribution change? Like would the burst usage still burn commit?

[07:17] Cole Summers: It depends on how the contract is structured. Usually baseline burns down commit. Burst is a separate line item, still Dedicated but priced differently.

[07:28] Priya Desai: We need simplicity. I’m fine with two line items but not, like, fifteen.

[07:34] Rachel Kim: Understood. We can propose a structure that’s pretty clean: base commit + burst addendum, and keep meters consistent.

[07:44] Ava Thompson: Another question: we’re also considering a second region because our EU team is complaining about latency. Does that affect burn-down?

[07:53] Rachel Kim: It can, because region is a dimension in the usage. It doesn’t inherently cost more per token, but if you deploy a second region with separate GPU pools, the commit may need to be split or you may need a larger total commit to cover both.

[08:08] Cole Summers: And on caching specifically, cache is region-local. So your cache hit rate will reset if you’re sending traffic to EU in addition to US.

[08:18] Miguel Santos: Right. Makes sense.

[08:21] Rachel Kim: Can we dig into the “token accounting under batching/caching” question a bit more? Miguel, what are you seeing?

[08:30] Miguel Santos: Yeah. So we do a large system prompt, like 1,200 tokens. Then we have a user prompt. With caching, I’d expect the 1,200 to show as cached and not count, or count differently. But what we see is: prompt tokens looks the same and then there’s extra “cache read tokens.” So when we sum, it’s bigger.

[08:52] Cole Summers: Got it. That’s a dashboard definition issue. The correct way is: total_prompt_tokens = prompt_uncached_tokens + cache_read_tokens. That equals what you think of as prompt tokens. Some views might show prompt_total plus cache_read separately, which double counts if you sum.

[09:13] Miguel Santos: So the console is confusing basically.

[09:16] Rachel Kim: In some pages, yes, especially older widgets. We’re aligning them. In the meantime, we’ll point you to the “Invoice-aligned usage” view and also I’ll send the burn-down export where columns are labeled the same as invoice.

[09:30] Priya Desai: Thank you.

[09:33] Ava Thompson: And batching—just to be crystal clear—you’re not like rounding up tokens because you batch.

[09:39] Cole Summers: Correct. There is no “batching tax.” Tokens come from the tokenizer applied to your input and the model output. Batching is just scheduling. Rounding can exist, but it’s not related to batching. If rounding exists it’s usually at invoice aggregation level or per-request minimums—again, depends on plan, but generally we don’t do per-request rounding for token meters.

[10:05] Miguel Santos: Ok.

[10:08] Rachel Kim: Another thing that can cause mismatches: model aliases. If you’re pinning “chat-large” but invoice maps it to the underlying model version, you might see different groupings. Not different totals, just different labels.

[10:21] Ava Thompson: We did change model versions last month.

[10:24] Miguel Santos: And we A/B tested quantized vs non, which also changed latency.

[10:29] Cole Summers: That can show up as different model IDs in telemetry, but totals still roll up. We can group by “model_family” to reduce noise.

[10:40] Priya Desai: Alright. So what do we need to do to reconcile? I want something that we can operationalize.

[10:48] Rachel Kim: I propose: you send us two to five representative request_ids where you see mismatches. One with caching, one streaming cancel, one retry scenario. Cole and I will pull the per-request usage record and show exactly which tokens were counted and why.

[11:07] Cole Summers: And if it helps, we can also export a daily aggregate by “request_outcome” so you can see if retries are significant.

[11:16] Miguel Santos: Ok. I can do that.

[11:20] Ava Thompson: One more: commit burn-down. Sometimes the burn-down report and the invoice preview don’t match for the same date.

[11:28] Rachel Kim: Yeah, that’s typically because invoice preview is after some late-arriving telemetry is included. Burn-down export is near-real-time. Also, if there’s a backfill or correction, invoice preview will incorporate it, burn-down might lag until next refresh.

[11:46] Priya Desai: So you do backfills.

[11:49] Cole Summers: Rarely, but yes. Usually if we fix a metering bug or missing dimension. We try to document it and keep it within agreed tolerances. For Dedicated, we coordinate before any backfill that would affect invoice materially.

[12:04] Ava Thompson: Ok.

[12:06] Rachel Kim: Switching gears to expansion. Ava, you mentioned end-of-quarter peaks. If we increased the commit by, say, 20%, would that cover it?

[12:18] Ava Thompson: Probably, but we need to see the projected curve. We’re adding a new feature that’s like a clinical note summarization flow. That might double traffic.

[12:30] Miguel Santos: It’s a lot of long contexts.

[12:33] Priya Desai: Which sounds like… more money.

[12:36] Rachel Kim: Potentially. But it also may benefit a lot from caching and batching. If the system prompt is stable and you have repeated templates, caching helps. And on Dedicated, you can tune throughput and cost more predictably.

[12:52] Miguel Santos: Are you charging for cache reads in Dedicated? Sorry, I know we already asked but it matters.

[12:57] Cole Summers: I’ll confirm. If cache reads are discounted, then enabling caching can materially reduce your spend. If not, it still helps our ability to keep latency consistent and handle peaks.

[13:11] Ava Thompson: Ok.

[13:13] Rachel Kim: For next week, I’ll draft two options: (A) bigger base commit, (B) base commit plus burst. We can also talk second region.

[13:23] Priya Desai: Please include a clean explanation of how burn-down is computed. I need to share with finance leadership.

[13:30] Rachel Kim: Will do.

[13:32] Miguel Santos: And if you can include like a sample invoice mapping to console fields, that would be nice.

[13:38] Rachel Kim: Yup. We have a template we can adapt.

[13:42] Ava Thompson: Also, we’re evaluating Bedrock for some workloads, mostly because procurement is already in AWS.

[13:49] Rachel Kim: Makes sense. From what we’ve seen, Dedicated with Redwood gives you more control over performance and routing, and you get the same support team. But happy to help you compare apples-to-apples.

[14:02] Miguel Santos: Our main issue with Bedrock is the model choice and some latency variability.

[14:07] Cole Summers: On Redwood Dedicated, you can pin versions and we can set SLOs. That’s usually the difference.

[14:15] Priya Desai: Ok.

[14:17] Rachel Kim: I want to make sure we cover your questions. Anything else on the token accounting side?

[14:24] Miguel Santos: One small thing: do you count tokens before or after any prompt compression? We do some internal truncation.

[14:32] Cole Summers: We count tokens as received by our API after any transformations you do client-side. We don’t do prompt compression unless you use an explicit feature that modifies the prompt, and that’s not in your current config. Truncation on your side will change the tokens we see.

[14:49] Miguel Santos: Ok.

[14:51] Ava Thompson: So basically to reconcile we should compare your “input_tokens” and “output_tokens” on the request record.

[14:57] Cole Summers: Exactly.

[15:00] Rachel Kim: Great. I’ll recap next steps before we drop.

[15:05] Rachel Kim: One: I’ll send a burn-down export Jan 15 through Feb 11, with breakdown by model and region, and definitions of billable tokens and what burns down commit.

[15:16] Rachel Kim: Two: Miguel or Ava will send two request_ids—one cached, one streamed cancel—so we can do per-request reconciliation.

[15:25] Rachel Kim: Three: Cole will confirm the cache token line item treatment under your current order form and billing config.

[15:34] Rachel Kim: Four: I’ll draft expansion options—bigger commit and/or burst capacity—and we’ll review next week.

[15:43] Priya Desai: Sounds good.

[15:45] Ava Thompson: Works for me.

[15:47] Miguel Santos: Yep, I’ll send request IDs.

[15:50] Cole Summers: Cool.

[15:52] Rachel Kim: Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up by email.

[15:56] Meeting ended.
